subtopics.title: Make a variable the subject
subtopics.exposition: A literal equation is an equation that has several letters or variables. Solving literal equations is also known as changing the subject of the formula. The area of a circle is an example of a literal equation: A = πr². The formula for speed is an example of a literal equation: v = D/t. The area of a triangle is A = ½bh. The height of a triangle is given by h = 2A/b. Literal equations are solved in terms of one variable. Solving literal equations uses the principles learnt about solving equations, applied to rearranging literal equations. To isolate the unknown variable, ask "what is it joined to?" and "how is it joined?" After finding what the unknown variable is joined to and how, perform the opposite operation to both sides as a whole. To isolate the required variable, rearrange the equation with that variable on one side of the equals sign and the rest of the variables on the other. To make h the subject of A = ½bh, the book rearranges to 2A = bh and then to 2A/b = h.

subtopics.title: Take out a common factor
subtopics.exposition: If the unknown variable is in two or more terms, take it out as a common factor. When R appears in more than one term, collect the terms containing R on one side: hr² = HR − hR. Take R out as a common factor of the terms on that side: hr² = R(H − h). After factorising, dividing by (H − h) gives R = hr²/(H − h).

subtopics.title: Clear denominators with the LCD
subtopics.exposition: If the unknown variable is in the denominator, multiply both sides by the lowest common denominator (LCD) and then continue to solve. To make R the subject of h = R × H/(R + r²), the first step clears the denominator R + r² by multiplying both sides by it, giving h(R + r²) = R × H. After clearing the denominator, continue to solve by expanding the bracket: h(R + r²) becomes hR + hr², giving hR + hr² = HR. LCD is the abbreviation for lowest common denominator.

claims.claim: A literal equation is an equation that has several letters or variables.
The area of a circle is an example of a literal equation: A = πr².
The formula for speed is an example of a literal equation: v = D/t.
Solving literal equations is also known as changing the subject of the formula.
Literal equations are solved in terms of one variable.
Solving literal equations uses the principles learnt about solving equations, applied to rearranging literal equations.
To isolate the unknown variable, ask "what is it joined to?" and "how is it joined?"
After finding what the unknown variable is joined to and how, perform the opposite operation to both sides as a whole.
If the unknown variable is in two or more terms, take it out as a common factor.
When the square root of both sides is taken, remember that there will be a positive and a negative answer.
If the unknown variable is in the denominator, multiply both sides by the lowest common denominator (LCD) and then continue to solve.
LCD is the abbreviation for lowest common denominator.
The area of a triangle is A = ½bh.
To isolate the required variable, rearrange the equation with that variable on one side of the equals sign and the rest of the variables on the other.
To make h the subject of A = ½bh, the book rearranges to 2A = bh and then to 2A/b = h.
The height of a triangle is given by h = 2A/b.
To make R the subject of h = R × H/(R + r²), the first step clears the denominator R + r² by multiplying both sides by it, giving h(R + r²) = R × H.
After clearing the denominator, continue to solve by expanding the bracket: h(R + r²) becomes hR + hr², giving hR + hr² = HR.
When R appears in more than one term, collect the terms containing R on one side: hr² = HR − hR.
Take R out as a common factor of the terms on that side: hr² = R(H − h).
After factorising, dividing by (H − h) gives R = hr²/(H − h).
